questions.stem: The HALOGEN family in the periodic table is found in which group?

options.option_text: Group 1, the alkali metals on the leftmost edge
Group 17, just before the noble gases on the right
Group 18, the rightmost group of noble gases
Group 14, the carbon family of elements

questions.explanation: Halogens — Group 17 (formerly VII A): Fluorine (F), Chlorine (Cl), Bromine (Br), Iodine (I), Astatine (At), Tennessine (Ts, synthetic). 7 valence electrons → eager to gain 1 to complete octet → form ⁻1 ions readily. Distractor 1 = alkali metals (Li, Na, K). Distractor 3 = noble gases (He, Ne, Ar). Distractor 4 = carbon family (C, Si, Ge).

questions.stem: At room temperature, which halogen is a LIQUID (the only halogen liquid at 25 °C)?

options.option_text: Chlorine, a yellow-green pungent gas
Bromine, a deep red-brown liquid
Iodine, a violet-grey solid that sublimes
Fluorine, a pale yellow gas, very reactive

questions.explanation: Phases at 25 °C: F (gas, pale yellow), Cl (gas, yellow-green), Br (LIQUID, dark red-brown — only one of the few liquid elements at room temperature, along with mercury), I (solid, dark violet, sublimes), At (solid, radioactive). Bromine vapour is highly toxic. Used in flame retardants, photography (silver bromide), pharmaceuticals.

questions.stem: Going DOWN the halogen group from F to I, the reactivity:

options.option_text: Increases gradually as atomic radius grows down the group
Decreases as atoms grow larger and bind electrons loosely
Stays approximately constant for every halogen species
Has no clear systematic pattern across the halogen group

questions.explanation: Halogen reactivity DECREASES down the group (F > Cl > Br > I). Reason: as atomic radius grows, the outer shell is farther from the nucleus → less attraction to gain an electron → less reactive. Fluorine is the most reactive non-metal known; reacts explosively with H₂ in dark; can corrode glass. Iodine is comparatively mild. Distractor 1 — opposite (atomic radius increases yes, but reactivity decreases). Distractors 3, 4 — false; trend is consistent.

questions.stem: CHLORINE gas is widely used to:

options.option_text: Sweeten swimming pool water for taste appeal
Disinfect drinking water and treat sewage at plants
Add a yellow tint to common household paints
Produce a sweet smell in indoor air conditioners

questions.explanation: Chlorine — strong disinfectant; used in municipal water + sewage treatment, swimming pools, bleaching of paper + textiles, manufacture of PVC, refrigerants (older CFCs, now phased out under Montreal Protocol due to ozone-depletion). Distractor 1 — chlorine doesn't sweeten; sometimes adds a slight chlorine smell/taste, removed by activated carbon. Distractor 3 — paint pigments are unrelated. Distractor 4 — opposite of true; chlorine has a sharp, pungent smell.

questions.stem: IODINE deficiency in the diet causes:

options.option_text: Beri-beri due to nutritional thiamine loss
Goitre, an enlargement of the thyroid gland
Scurvy, with bleeding gums and skin spots
Rickets, with softened bones in growing children

questions.explanation: Iodine — required for thyroid hormones T3 (triiodothyronine) and T4 (thyroxine). Deficiency → thyroid enlarges (goitre) trying to compensate; can cause cretinism in children, hypothyroidism in adults. India had high goitre belt in Sub-Himalayan zones; Universal Salt Iodisation (UPS) program since 1990s — iodised salt mandatory under Food Safety law. Distractor 1 = thiamine deficiency. Distractor 3 = vitamin C deficiency. Distractor 4 = vitamin D deficiency.

questions.stem: FLUORIDE is added to drinking water and toothpaste primarily to:

options.option_text: Improve the taste and smell of the water supply
Strengthen tooth enamel and prevent dental cavities
Make the water more transparent and clearer
Kill bacteria and viruses in the water source

questions.explanation: Fluoride — incorporates into tooth enamel (forms fluorapatite, more resistant to acid attack than hydroxyapatite) → reduces dental caries. WHO recommends ~0.7-1.0 mg/L in drinking water. EXCESS fluoride (>1.5 mg/L, common in some Indian groundwater belts — Andhra, Rajasthan) → DENTAL FLUOROSIS (mottled teeth) + SKELETAL FLUOROSIS (joint pain, bone deformities). Defluoridation a major rural-health concern. Distractor 1 — taste is incidental. Distractor 3 — fluoride doesn't affect transparency. Distractor 4 = chlorination's job, not fluoride's.

questions.stem: Halogens generally exist as DIATOMIC molecules (X₂). This is because:

options.option_text: They are too small to remain alone as single atoms
Each atom completes its octet by sharing one electron pair
They are always stable as monatomic species at room temperature
Pairing makes them gases at very high temperatures

questions.explanation: Each halogen atom has 7 valence electrons; needs 1 more for octet. Two atoms share one electron pair → single covalent bond → diatomic molecule X₂ (F-F, Cl-Cl, Br-Br, I-I). Same applies to other diatomic gases: H₂, N₂, O₂. Bond strength: F-F ≈ 158 kJ/mol (weakest among Cl, Br); Cl-Cl ≈ 243; Br-Br ≈ 193; I-I ≈ 151. Fluorine's anomalously low bond energy is due to electron repulsion in its small atom.
